title: The Founder's Hat

pages.text:
*From the Dropout Club Handbook, Rule 15: Normal is a setting on the oven, not a way to live.*

The Great Library was not a room. It was a canyon of books that had forgotten how to stand straight. Shelves rose higher than the village church steeple, connected by ladders that slid up and down with a soft, wooden whisper. Reading lamps floated nearby, drifting in lazy circles like fireflies that had lost their sense of direction.

Lulu leaned close to a shelf of thick, leather-bound encyclopedias. Several of them were snoring softly, a low, rhythmic rumble that vibrated in her teeth.

"I'm so sorry," she whispered, her voice trembling slightly. She adjusted her mismatched socks, one striped, one polka-dot, and tried to look apologetic.

Bunt, the troll, tiptoed behind her. His barrel boots were wrapped in soft cloth, and a red-spotted handkerchief the size of a tablecloth was stuffed firmly over his nose. His eyes were watering. The dust here was ancient and magical, and his allergies were screaming a silent, green-shouting alarm. He looked ready to sneeze, but he held it in with the focus of someone trying to catch a falling biscuit.

Marnie held a floating reading lamp high. The light caught the dust motes dancing in the air.

"Shh," she hissed, though her voice was as quiet as a mouse in a shoebox. "We are looking for the Charter."
pages.image: The Great Library of Humbleton Academy: towering bookshelves with sliding ladders, floating firefly-like lamps; Lulu with a black braid and orange hoodie whispering to snoring books, Bunt a tall troll in patched vest tiptoeing with a large red-spotted handkerchief over his nose.

pages.text:
They found the Founders' Section in a corner where the air smelled of old paper and dry leaves. A glass case stood on a pedestal of polished marble, gleaming under the lamplight, with a scroll of vellum inside that was so large it had to be rolled like a rug.

Toby stepped forward, his polished brown shoes clicking a steady rhythm on the stone. Click. Click. He adjusted his gold-rimmed glasses with a precise, delicate motion.

"Permission to inspect," he said, to no one in particular.

The glass case hummed, then unlocked with a soft click. He unrolled the scroll with the care of someone handling a sleeping cat. The ink was faded and brown, brittle as a dry leaf, but the words were clear.

"I, Wilhelmina Humbleton," Marnie read aloud, her voice echoing off the high ceiling, "in founding this school, enchant my hat to catch the overflow of perfect magic."

Lulu blinked. "Catch it?"

"For perfect magic has no room in it for wonder," Marnie continued, her eyes scanning the lines, "and will turn on itself."

Toby frowned, a small crease appearing between his eyebrows. "Turn on itself?" he said. "That sounds like a curse. Or a very bad joke."
pages.image: A glass display case containing a large rolled vellum scroll; Marnie with copper-red hair buns and green cloak reading aloud, Toby with gold glasses and navy vest inspecting the scroll, Lulu and Bunt looking on in the dim library light.

pages.text:
Marnie’s finger traced the final line of the text. The ink seemed to glow faintly, as if it remembered being wet.

"Only magic that is a little wrong can balance magic that is entirely right."

She read it once. Then she went very still. The air in the library felt thicker, charged with a sudden, electric silence. She looked at the scroll, then slowly turned her head to look at Gerald.

The goose was standing on the pedestal, his purple-and-silver-star ribbon bobbing. He looked at Marnie with a deep, offended dignity, his orange beak slightly open as if he were about to make a very reasonable point.

"He's not just a goose, is he?" Marnie whispered.

Toby lowered the scroll. "No," he said, his voice dry and flat. "He’s not."

Lulu gasped, her lavender-scented socks fluttering around her teal rain boots. Bunt lowered his handkerchief, his eyes wide and bright. The goose honked once, a short, sharp sound that cut through the silence like a knife through butter.
pages.image: Marnie looking intently at Gerald with a purple starred ribbon, standing on a marble pedestal in the library; Toby, Lulu, and Bunt watching from behind, the atmosphere tense and mysterious.

pages.text:
"The Principal's hat," Toby said, his mind working at full speed. "The tall purple one with the silver stars. He wore it for forty years. Every single day."

Marnie felt a cold prickle at the back of her neck. "It wasn't a hat. It was a sponge."

"A magical sponge," Lulu added, her voice barely a whisper. "For perfect magic."

Bunt nodded slowly, his moss-green hair tuft shifting. "Ah... it absorbs the overflow. The school was safe because the hat was there. Quiet. Invisible."

Marnie looked at Gerald. "I turned him into a goose. I took the sponge out of the machine."

Toby stepped closer, his expression serious. "You didn't ruin the hat, Marnie."

She looked up, her eyes wide. "I ruined everything."

"No," Toby said firmly. "You hid it. You changed its form. The magic is still inside. It’s just... wearing feathers right now."
pages.image: The four friends gathered around the glass case, Marnie looking at Gerald with realization, Toby explaining with a serious expression, the background of the library shelves fading into shadow.

pages.text:
Marnie straightened her cloak, her hands trembling slightly. "I can fix it."

The words fell out of her mouth before she could catch them. "I can turn him back. Properly. Once and for all. I just need to cast a perfect spell."

Toby’s face went pale. "No. If you cast a perfect spell, the hex will trigger. The gold wave will start again."

"I don't care," Marnie snapped, her voice sharp. "I care about fixing this. I care about being right for once."

Lulu and Bunt exchanged a worried glance. The goose honked, a low, rumbling sound that seemed to carry a weight of understanding.

The four of them stood in the dark library, the distance between them growing wider with every second. Gerald, standing between them, looked from Marnie to Toby, and back again. He honked quietly, a sound that was not quite a complaint, but not quite a promise either. It was the sound of a goose who knew he was in the middle of something very, very wrong.
pages.image: The four dropouts standing apart in the library, Marnie with an angry, determined expression, Toby looking concerned, Gerald looking between them, the mood heavy with unspoken tension.
